lesson.title: Where You Start and Stop: The Bounds That Frame an Integral
lesson.summary: The numbers a and b attached to an integral sign, the limits of integration, mark exactly where accumulation begins and ends, and they carry rules about orientation and splitting that follow directly from how the underlying sum is built.
lesson.body:
In the notation for the integral from a to b of f(x) dx, the number a written at the bottom is the lower limit of integration and the number b written at the top is the upper limit of integration. They are not decorations, they are literally the two endpoints of the interval that got sliced into subintervals when the Riemann sum was built. Change a or b and you are describing an entirely different accumulation, over a different stretch of the function's domain, with a different set of rectangles feeding the underlying sum.

Two structural rules follow directly from that origin. First, orientation: if you swap the bounds, the sign of the integral flips, so the integral from b to a of f(x) dx equals the negative of the integral from a to b of f(x) dx. This is not an arbitrary convention, it falls straight out of the definition, since running the accumulation backward from b to a makes each subinterval's width negative, which flips the sign of every term in the sum. Second, additivity: for any point c between a and b, the integral from a to b splits cleanly into the integral from a to c plus the integral from c to b. This makes sense because slicing the interval [a, b] into subintervals and slicing [a, c] and [c, b] separately and then combining them describes the exact same collection of rectangles, just grouped differently.

Here is a worked example showing additivity directly. Let f(x) = 2x on [1, 4]. Since f is linear, each piece is a trapezoid whose area is the average of the parallel sides times the width. Over the full interval, f(1) = 2 and f(4) = 8, width 3, so the integral from 1 to 4 of 2x dx = (2 + 8)/2 times 3 = 15. Now split at c = 3. Over [1, 3], f(1) = 2 and f(3) = 6, width 2, giving (2 + 6)/2 times 2 = 8. Over [3, 4], f(3) = 6 and f(4) = 8, width 1, giving (6 + 8)/2 times 1 = 7. Adding those pieces gives 8 + 7 = 15, matching the integral over the full interval exactly, which confirms additivity. Orientation follows the same numbers: the integral from 4 to 1 of 2x dx equals -15, the negative of the integral from 1 to 4.

These two rules are what make the integral sign notation from the previous chapter fully usable in practice. Additivity lets you break a complicated region into manageable pieces and reassemble the answer, and the orientation rule keeps the bookkeeping consistent no matter which direction you happen to be integrating. Both rules will resurface once the fundamental theorem gives a fast way to evaluate these integrals without building a Riemann sum from scratch every time.
